content.text: Computing Raises Legal and Ethical Questions

Computing has made it possible to create, copy, distribute, and modify digital content with extraordinary ease. This power raises important legal and ethical questions: Who owns digital content? When can you use someone else's work? What obligations do you have when you use it? Topic 5.5 addresses these questions through the lens of intellectual property, plagiarism, open licensing, and the broader legal and ethical concerns that computing innovations can create.

content.definition: Material created on a computer is the intellectual property of the creator or an organization. Ease of access and distribution of digitized information raises concerns about ownership, value, and use. Measures should be taken to safeguard intellectual property.

content.text: Intellectual property refers to creations of the mind — writing, code, music, artwork, inventions — that belong to their creators. Material created on a computer is the intellectual property of the creator or an organization. This is true whether the content is a novel, a song, a piece of software, a photo, or a research paper.

content.term: Why does digitization raise intellectual property concerns?
content.definition: Ease of access and distribution of digitized information raises concerns regarding ownership, value, and use. Digital content can be copied and shared almost instantly and for free, making it harder to protect the rights of creators.

content.text: Before digital technology, copying content required physical effort — a printing press, a recording studio, a photocopier. Each copy cost time and money. Digital technology changed this completely: a song, a book, or a software program can be copied perfectly and infinitely at essentially zero cost and shared with millions of people instantly. This ease of copying and distribution is what creates the intellectual property concerns the CED identifies.

rows: Copying requires physical effort, equipment, and cost
Copying is instant, perfect, and essentially free
Distribution requires physical logistics — shipping, stores, postage
Distribution is instant and global — email, websites, file sharing
Unauthorized copying is visible and limited in scale
Unauthorized copying can happen invisibly and at massive scale
Value is tied to the physical artifact
Value is in the information itself — separated from any physical form
Protecting rights is relatively straightforward
Protecting rights requires active technical and legal measures

content.definition: The use of material created by someone else without permission and presented as one's own. Plagiarism may have legal consequences. The use of material created by someone other than you should always be cited.

content.text: Plagiarism is both an ethical violation and potentially a legal one. The ethical violation is presenting someone else's work as your own — taking credit for ideas and effort that are not yours. The legal concern arises from copyright law — using copyrighted material without permission may violate the creator's legal rights.

The rule is simple: the use of material created by someone other than you should always be cited. This applies whether the material is text, code, images, music, or any other creative work. Citation gives credit to the creator and makes clear that the work is not your own.

rows: Using a paragraph from a website without citing it in your essay
YES — using material without permission, presented as own
Cite the source — include author, website, and date
Copying code from Stack Overflow into your program without attribution
YES — using code created by someone else without acknowledgment
Acknowledge the source in your code documentation
Using an open source library in your program
No — open source is designed for reuse
Still acknowledge it: note the library name and its license in your documentation
Quoting a few lines of a song in a paper with citation
No — citing gives credit to the creator
Always include citation information
Paraphrasing someone's idea without citing them
YES — presenting their idea as your own even without exact wording
Cite the source even when paraphrasing

content.label: Common Mistake
content.text: Plagiarism is not just copying word-for-word — using someone else's IDEAS without credit is also plagiarism. In programming, using code written by someone else without acknowledgment is plagiarism even if you modify it. The key question is: are you presenting someone else's work as your own? If yes, that is plagiarism regardless of whether you changed some of it.
Legal Ways to Use Others' Work
Not all use of others' work is plagiarism or illegal. The CED identifies three frameworks that allow legal use of others' digital content. All three have enabled broad access to digital information.

content.term: Creative Commons vs Open Source vs Open Access
content.definition:
Creative Commons: license allowing others to share, use, and build on copyrighted creative work.
Open Source: programs freely available to redistribute and modify.
Open Access: research output freely available with no access or use restrictions.
All three have enabled broad access to digital information.

A public copyright license that enables the free distribution of an otherwise copyrighted work. Used when the content creator wants to give others the right to share, use, and build upon the work they have created.
Programs that are made freely available and may be redistributed and modified.
Online research output that is free of any and all restrictions on access and free of many restrictions on use, such as copyright or license restrictions.

rows: Creative Commons
Creative works: photos, music, writing, art
Creator specifies what others can do — share, modify, use commercially, or only non-commercially, with or without attribution
A photographer publishes photos with a CC license allowing anyone to use them with credit
Open Source
Software and code
Anyone can view, use, modify, and redistribute the source code — often with certain conditions like keeping it open source
Linux, Firefox, and Python are open source software — anyone can view and modify the code
Open Access
Academic research and publications
Research papers and data available to anyone online for free — no subscription or payment required
Scientific journals that publish research freely accessible to anyone, not just institutions that pay for subscriptions

content.text: Creative Commons, open source, and open access have enabled broad access to digital information. Before these frameworks, most digital content was fully copyrighted by default — you needed explicit permission from the creator to use almost anything. These frameworks allow creators to proactively grant permissions, enabling a culture of sharing, building, and collaboration that copyright law alone did not allow.

content.label: Exam Tip
content.text: Know all three: Creative Commons = copyrighted creative work that the creator has licensed for sharing/use/building. Open Source = programs freely available to redistribute and modify. Open Access = online research output free of access and use restrictions. All three have enabled broad access to digital information. Even when using content under these frameworks, always cite the source.
Legal and Ethical Concerns from Computing Innovations

content.term: Legal and Ethical Concerns in Computing
content.definition: Computing can raise legal and ethical concerns including: software enabling digital media piracy, algorithms containing bias, computing used to harm individuals, and the digital divide. Computing can also play a role in social and political issues.

content.text: Using computing to harm individuals or groups of people raises legal and ethical concerns. Computing can play a role in social and political issues, which in turn often raises legal and ethical concerns. The digital divide raises ethical concerns around computing. These are not isolated issues — they are connected to broader questions about what computing should and should not be used for and how society should govern its use.

rows: Software that enables digital media piracy
Violates copyright law — creators have legal right to control distribution of their work
Harms creators who invested time and resources to create the work — taking without compensation
Algorithms that include bias
May violate anti-discrimination laws when used in employment, lending, or housing decisions
Perpetuates systemic inequality and causes unfair harm to individuals based on protected characteristics
Computing used to stalk or harass individuals
May violate stalking, harassment, and cybercrime laws
Violates the dignity, safety, and autonomy of targeted individuals
The digital divide
May implicate civil rights and equal access laws depending on context
Creates unequal opportunity and disadvantage based on socioeconomic status, geography, and demographics
Computing in social and political issues
Election interference, data collection by political campaigns may be legally regulated
Use of computing to manipulate public opinion or political outcomes raises democratic and ethical concerns
